questions.question: Jade recorded her quiz scores for the week: 6, 9, 9, 7, 10. What is the mode of this data set?
questions.explain: The mode is the value that appears most often; here 9 appears twice and every other value appears once. A common trap is picking a number like 7.5 that is not even in the data, or assuming the mode must be the smallest value.

questions.question: Sam rolls a fair 6-sided die and flips a fair coin. What is the probability of rolling a 5 AND getting tails?
questions.explain: Because the two events are independent, multiply their probabilities: 1/6 × 1/2 = 1/12. The most frequent error is adding (1/6 + 1/2 = 7/12) instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Mia counted the number of push-ups she did on 5 consecutive days: 14, 9, 14, 6, 22. What is the median?
questions.explain: Sort the data first: 6, 9, 14, 14, 22. The median is the middle (3rd) value, which is 14. A common mistake is to forget to reorder the numbers or to average the two 14s and write 14.5.

questions.question: Five students at a Vancouver school fundraiser donated $3, $8, $5, $7, and $7. What is the mean (average) donation?
questions.explain: Add all values (3+8+5+7+7 = 30) and divide by the count (5): 30 ÷ 5 = 6. The most common trap is reporting the median or mode (both 7) instead of the mean.

questions.question: A classroom game uses a 4-colour spinner (Red, Blue, Green, Yellow) and a fair 4-sided die (1, 2, 3, 4). How many outcomes are in the sample space, and what is the probability of getting Red AND rolling a 3?
questions.explain: The sample space has 4 × 4 = 16 outcomes. P(Red and 3) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Students often add the two probabilities (getting 1/2) or count the sample space as 4 + 4 = 8.

questions.question: Five friends recorded how many kilometres they cycled this week: 4, 6, 5, 7, 30 (one friend biked all the way to Vancouver). Which measure of central tendency is MOST affected by the 30 km value?
options: None — all measures are equally affected
questions.explain: The mean shifts dramatically (from 5.5 without the 30 to 10.4 with it), while the median (6) and mode (none) barely change. A common misconception is that an outlier affects every measure equally.

questions.question: At a school fair, you spin a 4-section spinner (Red, Blue, Green, Yellow) and roll a fair 6-sided die. You win a prize if you get Red AND an even number. Your friend Priya says, 'The chance is 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4, so it is really easy to win!' What is the correct probability, and is Priya right?
options: 1/8 — Priya is wrong; she added the probabilities instead of multiplying them
3/4 — Priya is correct because both events can happen at the same time
1/4 — only the spinner result determines the prize
1/2 — only the die result determines the prize
questions.explain: P(Red) = 1/4 and P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. For two independent events you multiply: 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8. Priya's mistake — adding instead of multiplying — is the single most common error with compound probability.

questions.question: A data set of 7 test scores is: 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 7, 9. A student writes: 'The mode is 5 because it appears first among the repeated values.' Which statement correctly identifies the mode and why?
options: The mode is 5 because it is the smallest value that repeats
The mode does not exist because no value appears exactly once
The mode is 7 because it appears more often than any other value
The mode is 6 because it is the midpoint between 5 and 7
questions.explain: Count frequencies: 7 appears 3 times, 5 appears 2 times, the rest appear once — so the mode is 7. The trap is to pick the first repeated value (5) or to confuse the mode with a midpoint/mean.
